title: Disturbia
full_review:
"Disturbia" (Paramount) is a reasonably suspenseful thriller in the tradition of Hitchcock's classic "Rear Window" with Shia LaBeouf as teenager Kale, the Jimmy Stewart-like protagonist.

In the film's opening, a gut-wrenching car accident kills Kale's adoring father. A year later, the young man's ongoing anguish results in him lashing out verbally at his mother (Carrie-Anne Moss) and punching an insensitive teacher.

Kale is summarily put under court-ordered house arrest for the summer. During this home incarceration, he begins to spy on his neighbors. Despite the modern technology available to him, Kale relies mostly on binoculars, and through his eyes we see several comedic but obviously objectionable images such as a married man carrying on with his maid and young kids watching cable porn. When the alluring Ashley (Sarah Roemer) -- with a penchant for wearing bikinis and other skimpy attire -- moves next door, Kale finds a new focal point.

Eventually, Kale starts to suspect next-door neighbor Mr. Turner (David Morse) might be a serial killer. Kale recruits Ashley and best friend Ronnie (Aaron Yoo) for some Hardy Boys-style sleuthing.

LaBeouf, who is in nearly every scene, carries the movie, though Roemer and Yoo have good moments.

Though its serial-killer theme may push the envelope for its intended teenage audience, director D.J. Caruso ("Taking Lives") can be credited with handling the violence -- restricted mostly to the last 10 minutes of the film -- in a relatively restrained manner, and putting the emphasis squarely on suspense rather than gore.

The film contains some violence including two murders, an image of a corpse and some discreet shots of other dead bodies, a disturbing car accident, some crude and crass language and profanity, skimpy costuming, underage drinking, suggestive dancing, and brief suggestions of infidelity and underage viewing of pornography. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
